purpose: Optional, formative practice suggestions from first attempts only; not a diagnostic or CEFR assessment.

grammar.title: Present simple and classroom questions
steps: For I, use am; for she or he, use is. In routines, add -s to he/she verbs.
Use do/does + subject + base verb to form present-simple questions.
grammar.example: Does Maya study physics? Yes, she does.

vocabulary.title: University learning words
steps: Identify the purpose of a lecture, notebook and laboratory session.
Practise useful collocations: take notes, attend a lecture, review your notes.
vocabulary.example: I take notes during the physics lecture.

reading.title: Find exact facts in a profile
steps: Read the question first, then locate the matching day, location or person in the source.
Answer only with information stated in the source. Reopen the reading if necessary.
reading.example: If the notice says 2:00 p.m., do not replace it with 12:00 p.m.

grammar.title: Articles, plurals and quantities
steps: Use a/an for a new singular countable object and the when the object is already known.
Equipment is uncountable; measurements are countable. Use how much for time and how many for measurements.
grammar.example: There is some equipment, and there are three instruments.

vocabulary.title: Correct SI unit names and symbols
steps: Match mass with kg, time with s, voltage with V, and temperature with K.
Keep case-sensitive SI symbols and insert a space between the number and its unit.

reading.title: Read numerical data carefully
steps: Return to the sample table and find the requested row or measurement.
Copy the quantity and the unit exactly; do not treat a demonstration as a real measurement.

mathematical-english.title: Scientific numbers in spoken English
steps: Read each digit after the decimal point: 0.05 is zero point zero five.
Distinguish thirteen (13) and thirty (30), and compare decimals by place value.

grammar.title: Existence, position and instructions
steps: Use there is with a singular item and there are with plural items.
Use this/these, that/those correctly, and keep directions relative to the supplied scene.
grammar.example: There are two timers next to the notebook.

vocabulary.title: Equipment and spatial descriptions
steps: Match equipment names to descriptions before placing them in a sentence.
Practise left/right, above/below, between and next to using the reading source.
vocabulary.example: The ruler is next to the notebook.

reading.title: Locate apparatus in the source
steps: Open the relevant room description and check the stated positions.
Do not invent a location that is not shown or described.
reading.example: Describe the source's arrangement, not an assumed real laboratory.

grammar.title: Habit versus action happening now
steps: Use the present simple for routines and usual behaviors.
Use am/is/are + -ing for what is happening at this moment.
grammar.example: The cart usually moves slowly. It is moving right now.

vocabulary.title: Motion and change verbs
steps: Select the verb matching the stated movement: rise, fall, turn, speed up or stop.
Do not infer a precise speed from an unlabeled picture.
vocabulary.example: The cart is moving to the right.

reading.title: Find tense clues in a text
steps: Look for now, at this moment, every week or usually.
Identify what the source explicitly describes and then select the tense.
reading.example: “Every Thursday” is a routine; “right now” is current.

grammar.title: Comparisons and sufficiency
steps: Use shorter than, longer than, higher than, or lower than to compare two quantities of the same kind.
Use as ... as for equal comparisons, and enough/too for suitability statements.

vocabulary.title: Measurement words
steps: Check the difference between length, mass, temperature and time.
Avoid claiming accuracy without a trustworthy reference measurement.
vocabulary.example: The second cable is longer, but no accuracy claim follows.

reading.title: Check both values before comparing
steps: Find the two numerical values and their units in the source.
Do not combine unrelated quantities or invent missing measurements.
reading.example: A difference of 20 cm is not 20 m.

grammar.title: Safety requirements and requests
steps: Must/have to express obligations; should expresses advice.
Must not prohibits an action; don't have to means it is not required. Could you...? is a polite request.
grammar.example: You must not look directly into a laser beam.

vocabulary.title: Read laboratory warning verbs
steps: Distinguish report, avoid, stop, ask and check in safety notices.
For actual equipment, always follow the instructor and locally applicable rules.
vocabulary.example: Report a damaged cable to an instructor.

reading.title: Separate notices from general advice
steps: Identify which instructions are requirements and which are recommendations.
Apply only the fictional scenario in the exercise; it cannot substitute for real lab safety rules.
reading.example: Must not is prohibition, not optional advice.

grammar.title: Completed actions in the simple past
steps: For a finished event, use the simple past rather than the present continuous.
Check regular -ed endings and irregular verbs such as take/took and write/wrote.
grammar.example: Yesterday, we recorded the simulated values.

vocabulary.title: Reporting procedure words
steps: Review verbs such as measured, recorded, checked and observed.
Distinguish what someone did from what the source shows.
vocabulary.example: We recorded a value; we did not establish a theory.

reading.title: Track the sequence of an experiment
steps: Use yesterday, first, next, then and finally to follow events.
Locate past actions from the source without inventing results.
reading.example: A source saying “checked” does not necessarily say “replaced”.

grammar.title: Past continuous and interruptions
steps: Use was/were + -ing for an action in progress at a past time.
Use simple past for a completed interruption, often introduced by when.
grammar.example: She was writing when the display went dark.

vocabulary.title: Describe a problem without guessing
steps: Use verbs such as stopped, restarted and appeared when the source supports them.
Separate the observed problem from an uncertain cause.
vocabulary.example: The display stopped responding; the cause was unknown.

reading.title: Identify simultaneous and interrupted actions
steps: Check which action was continuing and which event happened.
Read the when/while details before answering.
reading.example: “While she was watching” describes an ongoing action.

grammar.title: Present perfect versus simple past
steps: Use have/has + past participle to describe results relevant now, or experience without a finished time.
Use the simple past with explicit finished times such as yesterday or on Monday.
grammar.example: We have finished the table. We finished it on Monday.

vocabulary.title: Progress and experience language
steps: Distinguish already, just, yet, ever and never.
Use words that match the fictional progress report, not an invented experiment.
vocabulary.example: I have already checked the values, but I have not written the report yet.

reading.title: Check what was actually completed
steps: Search for evidence that a task is finished, pending or recently done.
Do not call a planned action a completed result.
reading.example: Not yet finished is different from already finished.

grammar.title: Causes, consequences and conditions
steps: Because gives a reason; so introduces a result.
Use present simple in an if-clause, and will + base verb for a possible future outcome.
grammar.example: If the model keeps the same rate, the position will increase.

vocabulary.title: Cause-effect vocabulary
steps: Review increase, decrease, lead to and result in using the provided model.
State assumptions before asserting a physics relationship.
vocabulary.example: The voltage increased in the fictional model.

reading.title: Follow the source's condition
steps: Find the model's assumption or if-statement first.
Avoid presenting model predictions as measurements.
reading.example: A predicted value is not an observed data point.

grammar.title: Future forms and cautious predictions
steps: Use will or be going to appropriately for predictions.
Use may or might when uncertainty is meaningful.
grammar.example: The graph may continue to rise if the same trend holds.

vocabulary.title: Graph and trend vocabulary
steps: Identify axis, slope, rise, fall and remain constant in a labelled graph.
Always name the quantity and unit together.

reading.title: Read the stated graph interval
steps: Identify the axes, units, displayed time range and numerical values.
Separate what the graph shows from what might happen later.
reading.example: A value at 5 s cannot be read from a graph ending at 4 s.

mathematical-english.title: Describe numerical changes clearly
steps: Increased from 2 to 5 states two endpoints; increased by 3 states the difference.
Check units before comparing and keep predictions separate from observed values.
mathematical-english.example: The value increased from 2 m to 5 m, a change of 3 m.

grammar.title: Combine A2 sentence patterns
steps: Use past forms for completed actions and present forms for descriptions of the current model.
Check that because, if and comparison sentences express the intended relation.
grammar.example: The graph rises because the modeled cart moves at a constant speed.

vocabulary.title: Report the virtual experiment accurately
steps: Use simulation, position, time, quantity and unit correctly.
Distinguish observation, assumption and prediction.
vocabulary.example: The virtual model displays a position of 3.0 m at 2 s.

reading.title: Recheck the project sources
steps: Find the model, procedure and numerical evidence in the corresponding source.
Do not turn simulated displays into claims about a real laboratory.
reading.example: The table displays a simulated value; it is not a physical measurement.

mathematical-english.title: Write complete graph data statements
steps: Read axis labels, a time and a position with correct units.
Describe the trend only across the displayed interval.
mathematical-english.example: Position increases from 0 m at 0 s to 4.5 m at 3 s.
